### Proof

#### 1.  Reformulating the condition

Put  

\[
X=a+d,\qquad Y=b-c,\qquad U=a-d,\qquad V=b+c .
\]

Then \(X>U>0,\;V>Y>0\) and a short computation gives  

\[
\begin{aligned}
X^{2}+Y^{2}&=(a+d)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}+2(ad-bc),\\[2mm]
U^{2}+V^{2}&=(a-d)^{2}+(b+c)^{2}=a^{2}+b^{2}+c^{2}+d^{2}-2(ad-bc).
\end{aligned}
\]

Hence

\[
ad=bc\iff X^{2}+Y^{2}=U^{2}+V^{2}.
\]

Therefore the original functional equation is equivalent to  

\[
\boxed{f(X)+f(Y)=f(U)+f(V)}\tag{1}
\]

for all \(X>U>0,\;V>Y>0\) satisfying \(X^{2}+Y^{2}=U^{2}+V^{2}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  A new function

Define  

\[
g(t):=f(\sqrt t )\qquad(t>0).
\]

With \(p=X^{2},\,q=Y^{2},\,r=U^{2},\,s=V^{2}\) the condition \(X^{2}+Y^{2}=U^{2}+V^{2}\) becomes  

\[
p+q=r+s .
\]

Equation (1) therefore rewrites as  

\[
\boxed{g(p)+g(q)=g(r)+g(s)}\tag{2}
\]

for all positive numbers \(p,q,r,s\) with the same sum.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  The sum depends only on the total

Fix a number \(S>0\).  
From (2) with \(r=s=S/2\) we get

\[
g(p)+g(S-p)=2g\!\Bigl(\frac S2\Bigr)\qquad(0<p<S). \tag{3}
\]

Thus for each \(S\) the value \(g(p)+g(S-p)\) is independent of the particular
\(p\); it depends only on the sum \(S\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  Jensen’s functional equation

Take any \(x,y>0\) and set \(S=x+y\) and \(p=x\) in (3).  We obtain

\[
g(x)+g(y)=2\,g\!\Bigl(\frac{x+y}{2}\Bigr)
\]

or, equivalently,

\[
g\!\Bigl(\frac{x+y}{2}\Bigr)=\frac{g(x)+g(y)}2\qquad \forall x,y>0. \tag{4}
\]

Thus \(g\) satisfies Jensen’s equation (mid–point linearity).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  From Jensen to additivity

Let \(h(t)=g(t)-g(1)\).  Then \(h\) also satisfies (4) and \(h(1)=0\).
From (4) we have \(2h\!\bigl(\frac{x+y}{2}\bigr)=h(x)+h(y)\); replacing
\(x+y\) by \(2z\) gives  

\[
h(z)=\frac{h(2z)}2 .
\]

Now for any \(x,y>0\),

\[
h(x+y)=2h\!\Bigl(\frac{x+y}{2}\Bigr)=h(x)+h(y). \tag{5}
\]

Thus \(h\) is additive on \(\mathbb R^{+}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.  Positivity forces linearity

Since \(f\) (hence \(g\) and \(h\)) is everywhere **positive**, the additive
function \(h\) is bounded from below on every non‑trivial interval.
A classical result for Cauchy’s equation states that any additive function
that is bounded on a set of positive measure (in particular on an interval)
must be linear.  Consequently there exists a constant \(\alpha\ge0\) such that  

\[
h(t)=\alpha t \qquad(t>0).
\]

Hence  

\[
g(t)=\alpha t+\beta \qquad\text{with }\beta=g(1)-\alpha .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 7.  Returning to \(f\)

Recall \(g(t)=f(\sqrt t )\).  Substituting \(t=x^{2}\) yields  

\[
f(x)=g(x^{2})=\alpha x^{2}+\beta ,\qquad x>0 .
\]

Because \(f\) takes only positive values, we must have \(\alpha\ge0\) and
\(\beta\ge0\) (if \(\alpha=0\) then \(\beta>0\)).  Conversely, for every such
pair \((\alpha,\beta)\),

\[
f(a+d)+f(b-c)-f(a-d)-f(b+c)=
\alpha\bigl[(a+d)^{2}+(b-c)^{2}-(a-d)^{2}-(b+c)^{2}\bigr]=0,
\]

the last equality holding because \(ad=bc\).  Hence these functions satisfy the
required condition.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Conclusion

All functions \(f:\mathbb R^{+}\to\mathbb R^{+}\) satisfying  

\[
f(a+d)+f(b-c)=f(a-d)+f(b+c)\qquad (a>b>c>d>0,\;ad=bc)
\]

are exactly the quadratic‑affine functions  

\[
\boxed{f(x)=\alpha x^{2}+\beta\qquad(\alpha\ge0,\;\beta\ge0,\;(\alpha,\beta)\neq(0,0))}.
\]

(If \(\alpha=0\) then \(\beta>0\); if \(\beta=0\) then \(\alpha>0\).)  These
indeed map positive reals to positive reals and are the only such solutions.<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
